extracted.intended_audience: public health authorities, emergency managers, risk communication professionals, policymakers and health-system planners
extracted.subtask_description: WHO guideline recommendations for designing, integrating and practicing emergency risk communication (ERC) in public health emergencies, covering trust-building, governance, information systems, capacity, finance, planning, social media and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust
rubrics_metrics.description: To build trust, risk communication interventions should link to functioning and accessible services, be transparent, timely, easy-to-understand, acknowledge uncertainty, address and engage affected populations, link to self-efficacy, and be disseminated using multiple platforms, methods and channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: clarity, timeliness, effective dissemination and transparency increase trust; harms occur when promoted actions cannot be performed because services are unavailable or difficult to access. Actions associated with higher trust include: acknowledging uncertainty (including forecasts/warnings); being transparent and not concealing negative information (e.g. casualty rates); rapid dissemination and intervention; creating easy-to-understand scientific communication; seeking public input and encouraging dialogue; ensuring coordination between health authorities and the media with a uniform message; avoiding rapid conflicting changes in information; and disseminating via multiple platforms. Consider local history with authorities and public perceptions; engage community members where appropriate (some local leaders may not be trusted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicating uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication by authorities to the public should include explicit information about uncertainties associated with risks, events and interventions, and indicate what is known and not known at a given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: failure to explain what is/is not known can cause harm. Uncertainty information must be consistent, non-contradictory, clear and easy to understand. While communicating uncertainty is generally associated with desirable outcomes (e.g. maintaining trust), there is potential for misunderstanding of likelihoods among both public and experts. Mass media emphasis on rapidly changing or contradictory information increases public uncertainty and may reduce trust. Authorities should carefully consider how to present uncertainty for different audiences (general public, vulnerable groups, stakeholders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Community engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify people whom the community trusts and build relationships with them and involve them in decision-making to ensure interventions are collaborative, contextually appropriate, and that the community owns the communication process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: inclusion of community members in planning improves preparedness and response. Implementation considerations: provide feedback as essential to engagement; involve community members in planning, information dissemination, training on roles/responsibilities, preparedness actions, and relationship building. Activities prior to an event engage communities more successfully than only during an event. Be attentive to context and culture; failure to understand context harms interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designate ERC role in governance and leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC should have a designated strategic role in global and national emergency preparedness and response leadership teams with well-defined roles and responsibilities for communication personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: designating ERC as a strategic role facilitates incorporation of risk communication as a functioning pillar of preparedness/response. Resource implications (training, hiring, paying risk communication professionals) are outweighed by benefit. Applies at local, national, regional and international levels. Mechanisms include placing ERC functions into national leadership, creating organizational proximity of ERC practitioners to leadership, and developing laws/policies/frameworks supporting ERC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop stakeholder and organizational networks (information systems and coordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and build on relevant stakeholder and organizational networks across geographical, disciplinary and, where appropriate, national boundaries to improve coordination and information flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: creation of task forces/committees with key stakeholders improves coordination. Resource implications include time, human and financial costs but benefits outweigh harms. Components for effective networks include existing relationships prior to incident; network-style teams rather than strictly hierarchical teams; use of information managers; and a public information officer. Leverage existing platforms (e.g. regional surveillance networks) and address technology gaps in resource-poor areas. Integrate NGOs and monitor relevant social media channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor information systems to users' needs and involve local stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor information and communication systems to users’ needs and involve local stakeholders to guarantee the flow of information across sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: involving local stakeholders improves information flows; potential harms include legal/policy restrictions on information release. Implementation consideration: ERC professionals need legislative and policy support where information release is restricted. Examples: centralize resources for culturally diverse communities; designate agencies with best geographical/community reach to lead information sharing; use local social networks for disaster risk reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity building (training and exercises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation and training of personnel for ERC should be organized regularly and focus on coordination across involved stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: training focused on inter-agency coordination improves ERC capacity. Implementation considerations: incorporate media training and include media representatives in exercises where appropriate; training should test ability to share information and develop coordinated interventions. Evidence notes gaps: exercises often lack post-action learning, social media instruction, blended formats, and evaluation training. Grey literature recommends annual refresher training, develop a cadre of trained personnel at local/national/regional/global levels, and train media personnel in crisis communication. Strengthen softer communication/interpersonal skills, analysis, monitoring and evaluation, stakeholder communications, sociopolitical/cultural analysis, and translation of technical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained financing for ERC
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC requires a defined and sustained budget that should be a component of core budgeting for emergency preparedness, response and recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Very low quality evidence). Rationale: limited direct evidence but grey literature indicates lack of funding hampered ERC in past crises (e.g. West African Ebola). Consider development of policies and mechanisms for sustained funding despite potential discussion sparsity in literature. Financing may be a challenge falling between development and relief funding streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic communication planning (best practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC planning must occur well in advance and be a continuous process with a focus on preparedness as well as response; it should be sensitive to stakeholders’ needs, participatory, responsive to context and incorporate feedback from affected groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice statement. Planning should: be collaborative with clearly defined roles/responsibilities; consider communities, cultures and lifestyles; identify multiple channels and means of communication; include training/information updates for communications personnel; pre-position communication resources (core messages, factsheets, discussion content); establish monitoring/assessment mechanisms to adjust messages; and involve affected communities in planning so they take ownership. Use contextual analysis, pretesting, feedback loops, and capture lessons learned. Distinguish evidence-based messages from uncertain ones and ensure early commencement of communication planning, including community assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and evaluation tools (research priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research is required to establish best mechanisms and methods for rapidly evaluating ERC interventions and incorporating evaluation findings and feedback from stakeholders and communities to inform and improve ongoing and future responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research recommendation. Rationale: GDG found no evidence supporting the effectiveness of current evaluation tools; establishing effective feedback loops is essential. Table 4 (not included here) lists currently used data-gathering tools by response phase which should be studied. Priority area for research to identify best monitoring/evaluation mechanisms and feedback incorporation into ERC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social media for engagement and monitoring (conditional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media may be used to engage the public, facilitate peer-to-peer communication, create situational awareness, monitor and respond to rumours, public reactions and concerns during an emergency, and to facilitate local-level responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditional recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: social media can engage public, monitor/respond to rumours, and facilitate local responses but contextual harms/limitations exist (misuse, cultural concerns, affordability). It encompasses varied tools (networking, photo/video sharing, live streaming, micro-blogging) with different affordances. Implementation considerations: train, employ and pay dedicated social media officers to build relationships, use social media consistently to build trust before/during/after emergencies, and use appropriate tools (e.g. WhatsApp, Twitter). Use hashtags that are organically used by the public rather than imposing new branded hashtags. Consider SMS, RapidPro and other mobile tools for reach in low-resource settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate social and traditional media for convergence of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media and traditional media should be part of an integrated strategy with other forms of communication to achieve convergence of verified, accurate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: integrating social and traditional media achieves information convergence and trust. Minimal resource implications identified. Implementation consideration: train, employ and pay dedicated social media officers; coordinate with press before and during incidents and remain available; integrate social media monitoring into overall communication strategy. Examples include use of Twitter/Facebook for myth-busting and leveraging partnerships (e.g. BBC+WhatsApp) to channel authoritative messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messaging: avoid technical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk should not be explained in technical terms, as this is not helpful for promoting risk mitigation behaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: technical language can confuse or prevent protective actions; non-technical language increases uptake. Messages should be clear, non-technical and culturally contextualized. Pretest messages with intended audiences and adapt as situation evolves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messaging: consistent, early messages from multiple sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent messages should come from different information sources and emerge early on in the emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: consistent messaging from multiple sources increases likelihood messages will be believed and acted upon; late messaging allows rumours to take hold. Coordinate among agencies to avoid conflicting information; ensure uniform messages across outlets and spokespeople where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messaging: promote specific, realistic protective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages should promote specific actions people can realistically take to protect their health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong recommendation (Moderate quality evidence). Rationale: specific, culturally and contextually appropriate actions increase mitigation behaviour; vague messages confuse people. Equity considerations: ensure recommended actions are realistic for vulnerable groups (e.g. people with disabilities). Implementation considerations (for all messaging recommendations): pretest with intended audiences, periodically review and reshape messages as the emergency evolves, adapt to cultural contexts, and provide mechanisms for feedback.
